speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (on behalf of the Prime Minister)
text: Since then, payment services have continued to evolve rapidly, with innovative activities and new business models emerging.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (on behalf of the Prime Minister)
text: One significant development is in the area of digital payment tokens, or DPTs.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (on behalf of the Prime Minister)
text: These are cryptocurrencies – such as Bitcoins – which are not denominated in any currency but can be used as a form of payment.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (on behalf of the Prime Minister)
text: The speed and cross-border nature of such DPT activities carry higher inherent money laundering and terrorism financing or ML/TF risks.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (on behalf of the Prime Minister)
text: They need to be regulated and service providers need to carry out proper customer due diligence and monitoring of transactions.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (on behalf of the Prime Minister)
text: Global standards setting bodies, regulators and policy makers around the world are focused on addressing these risks.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (on behalf of the Prime Minister)
text: As a major financial centre and fintech hub, Singapore has played an active role in shaping international standards, including at the Financial Action Task Force, or FATF, which sets standards for combating ML/TF.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (on behalf of the Prime Minister)
text: The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) is therefore enhancing its regulatory framework and updating the PS Act to keep pace with changes to international standards and to better mitigate ML/TF risks related to DPTs.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (on behalf of the Prime Minister)
text: MAS has conducted a public consultation on the Bill and noted the broad support from respondents.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (on behalf of the Prime Minister)
text: MAS has considered the feedback received and, where appropriate, has taken them into account in finalising the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (on behalf of the Prime Minister)
text: The Bill makes amendments to the PS Act in three broad areas.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (on behalf of the Prime Minister)
text: Under the PS Act, MAS currently regulates service providers dealing in DPTs and facilitating the exchange of DPTs where the service provider comes into possession of monies or DPTs.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (on behalf of the Prime Minister)
text: These are common business models of DPT service providers that operate in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (on behalf of the Prime Minister)
text: The scope of the PS Act will be expanded under this Bill to confer on MAS powers to regulate service providers of DPTs that facilitate the use of DPTs for payments and may not possess the monies or DPTs involved.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (on behalf of the Prime Minister)
text: The FATF standards term these service providers as virtual asset service providers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (on behalf of the Prime Minister)
text: This will help minimise the risk of DPT service providers being exploited by criminals to launder illicit proceeds or hide illicit assets.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (on behalf of the Prime Minister)
text: The Bill will also pre-emptively address ML/TF risk that is outside of the DPT space.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (on behalf of the Prime Minister)
text: That way, such service providers will come under the regulatory ambit of MAS even if the monies do not flow through Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (on behalf of the Prime Minister)
text: The second set of amendments provides MAS with powers to impose measures on DPT service providers to ensure better consumer protection and to maintain financial stability and safeguard the efficacy of monetary policy.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (on behalf of the Prime Minister)
text: The risks to consumers are not significant currently because of the relatively low usage of DPTs in Singapore today.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (on behalf of the Prime Minister)
text: However, user adoption of DPTs could gain traction quickly as the industry comes out with products to attract customers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (on behalf of the Prime Minister)
text: We have seen recent development of new forms of DPTs which values are pegged to stable assets to gain users' confidence.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (on behalf of the Prime Minister)
text: It is therefore important for MAS to be able to respond to market developments and address new risks in a timely manner.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (on behalf of the Prime Minister)
text: This will augment current powers that allow MAS to require DPT service providers to safeguard customer money from loss in the event of insolvency.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (on behalf of the Prime Minister)
text: MAS will also be empowered to impose additional measures on certain DPT service providers to maintain stability in Singapore's financial system, safeguard the efficacy of the monetary policy or where it is in the interest of the public to do so.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (on behalf of the Prime Minister)
text: The scope of this new power is necessarily broad so that MAS can respond flexibly and swiftly in the fast-moving DPT landscape.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (on behalf of the Prime Minister)
text: MAS will consult the public and the industry when drafting subsidiary legislation on the specific measures.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (on behalf of the Prime Minister)
text: As financial institutions are sophisticated entities that can protect themselves, the Act carves out the situation where a financial institution is part of the transaction.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (on behalf of the Prime Minister)
text: However, that means that an individual involved in a domestic money transfer transaction with a financial institution is not accorded protection under the Act.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (on behalf of the Prime Minister)
text: The Bill will therefore broaden the scope of protection of the PS Act to carve out only situations where both payer and payee are financial institutions.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (on behalf of the Prime Minister)
text: With the fast-evolving landscape, user protection concerns associated with other types of licensees can also arise.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (on behalf of the Prime Minister)
text: The Bill will thus allow MAS to prescribe, where necessary, additional classes of licensees conducting specific payment services to be subject to the requirement to safeguard customer money.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The fight against money laundering and terrorism financing is the fight to make sure that crime does not pay.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This mission, by necessity, must include all players of our finance industry.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Before I continue, let me thank MAS for conducting a public consultation which shaped the proposed amendments we see today.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Public consultations help us formulate better policies and I hope MAS will continue this good practice.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have three points of clarification to make on this Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is about anonymity in our payment eco-system.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This removes one benefit of cryptocurrency, which is its anonymity.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I will say, first, that I fully agree with the intent of this Bill – bad actors must not be allowed to use Singapore's financial system for their purposes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But cryptocurrency's quest for anonymity is perhaps one we can empathise with.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: You cannot access any digital services without someone storing every little bit of information about where you are, what you do and who you are.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Today's world is also plagued by massive data leakages and malicious hackers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A month does not go by before some company we know spills our private information and order history into the wild.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Bill provides powers for MAS to enact regulations on licensed DPT service providers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many of the regulations pertain to the DPT service provider's maintenance of and safeguarding of assets belonging to users.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It helps keep our financial system stable and it protects the assets of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As part of its efforts to protect users, will MAS consider introducing other forms of user protection measures?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In particular, will MAS consider regulating DPT servicer providers to ensure they do not engage in misleading or deceptive conduct concerning their offerings?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Service providers will likely latch onto these qualities when marketing to unsuspecting consumers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Regulating how DPTs at an earlier point when they are marketed to consumers would complement regulations at a later stage on money management by service providers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: After all, it will be harder to defraud or otherwise harm a customer who knows what they are getting themselves into.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third point relates to the illegal wildlife trade.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This Bill expands our regulatory scrutiny of international money transfers and that is a good thing.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In this spirit, I ask that we work more closely with financial institutions to ensure that their internal controls can accurately identify signs of illegal activity, particularly when it comes to illegal wildlife trade.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is not a new idea from me.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is a best practice recommended in a June 2020 report by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF), titled "Money Laundering and the Illegal Wildlife Trade".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I quote, "There is a need for both the public sector to share additional information with reporting entities, including feedback on   filed, and for reporting entities to review whether current internal controls against money laundering from the illegal wildlife trade are in line with identified risks...

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Where competent authorities have shared information, financial institutions have been able to incorporate this into their transaction monitoring systems and, in turn, provide richer intelligence for  ." My team spoke to some employees of local financial institutions who monitor transactions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Some shared their concerns that they may only receive generic responses from the authorities with regard to the suspicious transaction reports they file.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One, the employees do not know whether the signals they are looking out for are relevant or not.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The feedback from the authorities with regard to the suspicious transaction reports is not specific enough to motivate meaningful operational changes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Two, the employees have little information on the status or outcomes of Government investigations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This means they struggle to take internal follow-up actions to adjust the risk levels of these clients.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Better feedback will help our Government get more relevant reports as well as help financial institutions take strong internal actions against bad actors.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: At a seminar held by the Association of Certified Anti-Money Laundering Specialists (ACAMS) last October, the panelists from the industry noted that there has not been sufficient focus on the financial aspect of tackling the illegal wildlife trade.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To ensure that its feedback is relevant, will the Government also consider holding discussions with ground staff at financial institutions to assess the efficacy of its existing feedback?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: To preserve that, we have to ensure that our regulations strike the right balance between carefully managing risks and encouraging innovation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: E-money has also received high adoption rates here and our consumers need to be protected.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Seventy-seven percent of Singaporeans already used digital wallets, though there is still much room for improvement in the adoption of digital payments, as my Parliamentary colleague, Mr Louis Chua Kheng Wee we will expand on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We have to ensure consumer confidence has not misplaced.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Trust in business is also earned and this is where a sound regulatory framework plays a crucial role.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The Payment Services (Amendment) Bill is a step in the right direction of proactive regulation of the payment space.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I declare my interest as the CEO of a Research Consultancy that undertakes work in the fintech space, among other sectors.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The expanded definition of DPT service provider will capture entities who offer token custody services or entities will market or advertise token sales.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Such entities will have to be licensed and regulated to the same extent as a token exchange.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Here, I would like to note in passing, that my parliamentary colleague, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim will be making a similar argument in the context of the moneychangers actor and small businesses.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, a token marketer or token custodian such as, a wallet service provider, for example, may not pose the same risks as a token originator or a token exchange to warrant such regulation by the MAS PSNO requirements.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Specifically, for a token marketer limb E of the proposed inclusion, states that an entity who induces a person to buy or sell a DPT ought to be regulated, although this entity may not come into possession of the DPT at all.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: While some marketing may be performed by a DPT custodian, other entities such as, for example, a professional public relations company asked to design or execute an ICO campaign or even a blogger writing about hot ICOs, may conceivably be caught in the net.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: What then is the purpose of requiring such an entity to meet periodic returns and our audit requirements if they are merely in the service of marketing a token and might it be too onerous for such an entity to meet the whole suite of MAS PSNO requirements?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Also, industry feedback suggests that the definition of arranging or inducing an individual to enter into a transaction is vague.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Perhaps, the Minister could provide further clarifications on the exact types of activities that fall within the definition of "arrange" or "induce".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: On token custodians, there are also concerns from stakeholders in the DPT space that the definition of control in the proposed limbs F through H is somewhat vague.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: While MAS had clarified that I quote, "A DPT service provider will have control of a DPT if it has the ability to control access to any DPT or to execute transactions involving the DPT", further regulatory guidance as to what this control exactly is, would be helpful.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I would also suggest that MAS consider in the fullness of time offering relaxation on MAS requirements, for entities who pose less of a threat.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, relaxing the audit requirements or periodic returns requirements for a token advertiser.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In the prior crypto wave in 2017, companies who dealt in digital tokens were required to hold a capital markets licence if such tokens resembled security or shares.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Now, these companies have to also hold a major payment institutional licence or standard payment institutional licence under the PSA, if the tokens that they custodise hold the payment function.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Perhaps, more guidance and defining incidentality would be helpful for entities to make an assessment as to whether a token's payment function is merely incidental to its core business function of providing custodial service.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In addition, Sir, it is unclear who the onus is on to determine whether a token is a DPT or not.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Whether that falls on the custody service provider to assess whether a token it seeks to custodise is a DPT thus having a payment function warranting a licence application, or whether it falls on the token originator to warrant that its token is not a DPT and thus the custody service providers have no need to apply for a PSA licence.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, must a wallet service provider conduct its own analysis as to whether a token that it seeks to custodise falls under the definition of a DPT under the PSA or whether it may carry out its custody service, as long as the DPT provider is already a licence entity?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Perhaps, there should be further consideration as to whether the PSA should provide an exemption for custody service providers in the event that the token issuer is already licensed.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: While consumer protection is an important concern, feedback from the industry, especially smaller firms, suggest that this is a cause for concern by them.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For instance, the proposed amended section 21(A) may be too onerous in the view of some in the industry.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It should be borne in mind that excessive regulation could curb entrepreneurship in a sunrise industry and crowd out smaller players and start-ups leaving only the bigger players to dominate.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This in turn would be bad for entrepreneurship and innovation in the longer term.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Thirdly, Sir, the expanded definition of cross-border money transfer services raises questions in terms of its enforceability and benefits for Singapore, in terms of congruence with other competing jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This amendment Bill expands the definition of cross-border money transfer service to require licensing of service providers like brokers in Singapore that actively facilitate cross-border money transfers between entities in different countries, although monies are not accepted or received in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Under the current PSA, such providers are not covered.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: While it is laudable that Singapore is taking the lead on cross-border regulation of VASPs and adopting FATF recommendations, there are two concerns.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: How does the Government intend to monitor and enforce this?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: While according to an FATF review and I quote, "Twenty jurisdictions advised that they have extended their regime to include value-added service providers or VASPs conducting operations from their jurisdiction", the review did not appear to identify the specific jurisdictions or provide specific details about these regimes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Furthermore, the review then noted that such a diversity in approach and I quote, "may present challenges in identifying which VASPs are regulated by each jurisdiction".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In respect of other jurisdictions specifically, for instance, there do not appear to be similarly expansive definitions, which have been implemented or proposed with regard to cross-border money transfers in Hong Kong or the Cayman Islands, even though these jurisdictions have proposed to enact or have enacted legislation in connection with the FATF guidelines.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Hence, I would like to ask if the MAS will, going forward, monitor the extent of international regulation of VASPs in line with the FATF recommendations and calibrate the onerousness of our own regime in line with what is being done internationally, with an eye to our competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Fourthly, Sir, I would like to speak about the need for greater transparency and less of a black box approach in the payment service licence application process.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The payment service licence process required for firms covered under the PSA is perceived by some industry players as a completely black box.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Many companies reportedly find themselves stuck on the waiting list for long periods.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Moving beyond a completely black box approach to a greater degree of transparency, could provide more support to viable businesses to get licence and go to market faster.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It may also enhance Singapore's attractiveness as a fintech Hub.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: While MAS does provide some basic criteria, for example, base capital requirements, fit and proper requirements of shareholders and employees, no entity is familiar with the actual determining factors that make or break a licence application.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Companies may apply for exemption status to continue operating on a small scale for six months while waiting for the licence but cannot scale up during that time.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And there are likely even more in the pipeline, namely those who directly applied for the licence without seeking exemptions, those who are still seeking legal advice and have not yet applied, and those who will only apply after this amendment passes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: While it is understandable that the full licensing criteria cannot be disclosed due to the risk that some applicants may game the system, as it were, this has to be balanced against the need for some transparency, so as to enhance Singapore's attractiveness as a fintech hub.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: With that in mind, I would like to ask the Minister for information regarding the proportion of successful applicants to total number of applicants and the average duration companies have had to wait for an outcome.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I would also like to ask if the MAS would consider providing: (a) a clearer fixed timeline and process including an appeal process so applicants know when to expect an outcome; (b) more resources to help innovative businesses understand and navigate the licencing process.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For instance, project innovate by the UK's financial conduct authority targeted support to innovative businesses in navigating the FCAs at the authorisation process.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 5.35 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 5.15 pm until 5.35 pm.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While I understand the premise behind the proposed amendments with regard to scope to essentially ensure adequate regulatory coverage of the Bill to all MAS licensees, I wish to raise three cautionary points, all related to potential unintended consequences.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Before I proceed, I wish to declare that I am the Chief Economist (Emeritus) of a homegrown investment advisory firm, which had previously been involved in payment services.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For changes set forth in clause 4, the applicability of the Bill to payment services providers that hold either moneychanging, standard payment institutions or major payment institution licences, there is also the need to take into account current economic realities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While the latter two groups have, by and large, rode through the pandemic relatively unscathed, this is not the case for moneychangers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I have residents operating such businesses that have reported declines in business of up to 90% and who do not anticipate any improvement to business in the months ahead.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Clause 7(e) seeks to widen the scope of digital payment token service providers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Understandably, it attempts to cast a wide net.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is worth cautioning, however, that by defining such providers broadly, a number of very small players may unfortunately be caught in this expanded regulatory net.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For instance, stipulating that any service involved in accepting digital payment tokens is unobjectionable if applied to large clearing houses, but it becomes a concern if it is applied to small-time intermediaries collecting payments on behalf of his or her clients.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As another example, a service arranging the transmission of digital payment tokens sounds appropriately targeted at custodians and brokers but may raise awkward questions of whether Cousin Angie by doing her Uncle Victor a favour by storing some of his e-cash in her digital wallet may inadvertently find herself subject to MAS rules, if she also happens to be a licensee.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In the public consultation process, I believe that MAS has indicated that the law's applicability is "fact dependent", and I quote here, and it is based on, again quote, "detailed assessment of activities" and would generally apply to agents that are already currently subject to licensing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My colleague, Mr Leon Perera has spoken more extensively about the detrimental effects of over-regulating small players, especially insofar as stifling innovations is concerned.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In remote villages in developing countries, a local youth may routinely play the intermediary role.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such actions ultimately gave birth to formidable national institutions like M-Pesa in Kenya and Grameen Bank in Bangladesh.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While Singapore is not a developing economy, a payment services law that does not consciously allow regulatory forbearance for small and medium enterprises may overburden these emerging firms with compliance to the long shadow of the law and hence stifle their growth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Relatedly, as far as I can gather, the legislation will treat all digital payment tokens equally.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Well, there is merit in not picking a specific privately issued DPT to support, it strikes me as odd that the same treatment is extended even to official DPTs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, we currently afford special status to official fiat currency as we should, not least to our local money, the Singapore dollar.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And so, as long as there is not any fraud, it is entirely reasonable to privilege an MAS-issued DPT.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This would serve to further undermine their confidence in digital payments where a number have already had negative experiences due to unscrupulous customers that have defrauded them and weakened their overall willingness to actively participate in the digital economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Notwithstanding these legislations, Mr Deputy speaker, I offer my support for the proposed amendments.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, allow me to raise some considerations in its implementation from a more social perspective, especially to safeguard more vulnerable user segments.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The group of users that I am most concerned about are the seniors because of the good, the bad and the unintended developments in the digital payment token service space.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has changed the way we socialise and interact with each other.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: From how we work and play to how we make purchases for our daily needs, almost every aspect of our life has been impacted in one way or another.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The need to reduce human contact has accelerated the need and pace for digitalisation.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Financial services have been going cashless and moving online with more new types of players beyond the traditional financial institutions with more sophisticated financial products, such as the DPT that is fast innovating and growing.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This acceleration, though challenging, is generally good for the economy at large and also helps the public to keep pace with digitalisation.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is timely, especially when the accelerated shift of financial services towards the digital will also likely increase the risks of misuse of such services and scams.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The amendments will further ensure responsible and safe innovation in the financial services industry.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While accelerating digitalisation, such as the DPT innovation and development, is good for the economy, it has also exposed an uneven understanding and adoption of technology among segments of the population, especially the seniors.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The closure of physical touch points has accelerated banking and payment services online and, overnight, the seniors needed to learn how to transact with banks and merchants digitally.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Research in the seniors' perceptions towards digital payment is sparse and is specific to countries.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Nonetheless, taking reference from a report published in November 2018 by AgeUK, those aged 65 and above who are online appear to place a higher emphasis on communication and information-finding and less on transactions, such as internet banking, needless to say sophisticated products like digital payment token transactions.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Closer to home, the 2019 IMDA Annual Survey on Infocomm Usage in Households and by Individuals also highlighted that while there was a considerable increase in Internet usage by seniors aged 60 and above, this same age group registered the lowest proportion for payment activities, such as transferring of funds, using online payment services, Internet fund transfers, peer-to-peer fund transfers and having an eNETS virtual account.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Not surprisingly, seniors were also the largest group that did not have the confidence in making online transactions and had the lowest level of trust that their privacy and data will be respected when performing online transactions.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In both these reports, the seniors' lack of trust, privacy concerns and lack of skills and confidence in being able to navigate the online world have been cited as reasons for them not going online and interacting digitally.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The unintended consequences would be that, firstly, the seniors may begin to lag in the adoption of digital payment services and this gap may continue to widen as the acceleration towards digitalisation increases with new innovations in the payment services space.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If we do not actively work to include the seniors, they could find themselves excluded from some important financial services or, worse, getting themselves involved in financial transactions or transfers, including cross-border ones, without fully understanding the risks of being used in crimes like money laundering or scams.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We can also expect new digital payment platforms, new service providers and new technologies that will be introduced.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The seniors will not only have to contend with a steep learning curve but also with having to choose which platform to use.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We need to educate, build trust and confidence towards digital payment services with these seniors.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As a nation, we need to continue to break new grounds so that we can take advantage of opportunities even in uncertainties and challenges.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I look forward to seeing new digital banking and payment service regulations that will enable an industry to develop products that will make lives of Singaporeans easier and more fulfilling, done in a responsible, inclusive and safe way.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On that note, Mr Deputy Speaker, I support the amendment Bill.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, such alternatives to physical cash can promote digital financial literacy and economic efficiency.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This amendment Bill, in my view, represents progressive legislation and I commend the focus on identifying potential incremental risks covering broad areas that include financial stability, monetary policy and also financial crime prevention – in particular, anti-money laundering and countering the financing of terrorism.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: There is also some focus on technology risks, which include risks around data.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Apart from seeking the Minister's assurance that there will be a robust requirement of anti-money laundering tools to ensure token purity checks and so on so that tokenised payments are not misused for illicit purposes, it is on the theme of technology and data, which is fundamental to digital payment service providers, that I would like to identify incremental risk areas which I feel are known or reasonably foreseeable and, therefore, warrant more attention and strengthening.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I reflect on recent examples in Singapore that were reported in the media, such as KuCoin, a Singapore-headquartered digital asset exchange and Grab.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Industry observers noted this to be the third largest crypto hack in history.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In its September report, the technology magazine CPO headline read, I quote, "Fourth privacy breach in two years for Grab.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Given low fines, does the company have a reason to care?" Unquote.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Before I go on, I want to emphasise that there is regulatory scrutiny by the Monetary Authority of Singapore and the Personal Data Protection Commission, which have made considerable efforts to balance the bright future of technology and data with its attendant risks.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: What I am saying is that the rate of change in this area should spur us on to greater efforts.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Today, we already know that no technology security is fool-proof and we now see exponential use of AI, cloud infrastructure, the emergence of 5G and quantum computing.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: These developments have deep implications on the future of cybersecurity and responsible use of data and demand a corresponding requirement to uplift our population.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This rate of technology change is accompanied by a concern which we need to remember that, payments fintech, on its own, is driven fundamentally by investor valuations.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: It is well understood that profit margins are thin in the payment services.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: So, such firms strive to create a data eco-system in the hope of profiting from adjacent businesses.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This is where technology risk management could be relegated to a lower priority until a hack happens.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This is no different from how our other regulators do this, such as the Singapore Food Agency providing food hygiene ratings to hawker stalls or the Building Construction Agency providing the Quality Mark and performance scores of developers and contractors to help homebuyers make informed decisions.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In this way, ordinary consumers can easily understand and make their own informed assessment when selecting payment providers even as we make more efforts to upskill their digital literacy.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This can help ensure that industry players are culturally attuned from day one and ensure that digital public education is as much the responsibility of industry players as it is the Government's.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As a related point, as we think through these issues, I advocate that we continue to maintain our successful whole-of-Government approach to regulate and ensure that the no material systemic issues fall through the cracks between areas of responsibility.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: We should move boldly, but skillfully execute with a commitment to manage known or foreseeable risks.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):    I rise in support of the Payment Services (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With the amendments, Singapore will have one of the clearest and most pragmatic regulatory frameworks in the world to manage cryptocurrency services.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Digital payment token service providers now have a complete rule book to comply with the MAS’ licensing requirements.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We will be able to position ourselves as a progressive destination for financial investors and service providers in both the digital and traditional asset sectors.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Greater regulatory clarity would be attractive to global crypto businesses.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In English): As virtual asset service providers will need to perform screening, customer due diligence (CDD), collection of Know Your Customer (KYC) information from platform users, transaction monitoring and reporting, and record keeping, there will be greater transparency and trust in the system.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Higher public confidence will be beneficial to the developments and innovations in this sector.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hence, I would like to ask if MAS can prescribe a centralised or integrated platform for the DPT service providers to research on the transaction details, share information and improve efficiency.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Anti-money laundering and countering terrorist financing requires DPT service providers to monitor cross-border value transfers and collect alternative CDD information.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Some of these transactions may involve physical goods movement.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Collection of transaction information is not that difficult, especially when the criminals have the intention to launder money.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is important for the DPT service providers to comply with the spirit of the regulations and assess if the information furnished makes business sense.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Money launderers inflate the transaction values to move their funds, in our case, it will be the DPTs, around.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, if a pair of Hello Kitty soft toys are valued at $50,000 and the client explains that these are limited edition ones, how does the service provider authenticate the value of these Hello Kitties?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would MAS prescribe that the service providers must invest in search engines like international maritime bureau (IMB) systems which can track and authenticate shipments, or Bloomberg systems so that the commodity prices can be verified?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We must not allow the collation of customer due diligence process to become a box-ticking exercise.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Next, I would like to voice my support for the new user protection measures.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is important to protect individual investors and consumers who may be encouraged to invest in digital tokens.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The recent gravity-defying rally of Bitcoin shows that it and other cryptocurrencies are getting more widely accepted as an asset class.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: At the same time, the crash of XRP is a reminder that, all over the world, governments are trying to figure out how to regulate this sector.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: MAS’ risk-based supervisory approach provides greater user assurance and regulatory safeguards for areas with high risks, and unregulated spaces to allow exploration of improvements and more efficient approaches.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They can maintain a stable value relative to another asset or a basket of assets.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would the Ministry require capital adequacy ratios, similar to those for banks, for DPT service providers to protect the DPT depositors?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This amendment Bill is yet another milestone in Singapore’s digital payments landscape in our journey to becoming a Smart Nation.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Broader implications include investor protection, consumer protection, data and privacy, systemic risk, monetary risk policy and national security.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A few jurisdictions have initiated regulatory reforms to address digital payment tokens as a means of payment.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Whether Singapore will accept a token-based payment system on a wider scale remains to be seen.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Nonetheless, I am heartened by the Government’s support for innovation in this area.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am confident that the Bill will help strengthen industry-Government partnerships and lead to new investments and businesses here in the years to come.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In the era of e-payments, and with DPTs gaining popularity worldwide, this is a necessary move.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Fintech is an integral component of our Smart Nation vision.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Singapore's friendly position on cryptocurrencies will attract tech start-ups and businesses here.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Stepping up on regulations would elevate our status as a global cryptocurrency and blockchain hub.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Regulating DPTs will be welcomed by industry professionals.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I believe that after the Bill is passed, we may see an uptick in businesses accepting cryptocurrencies as payment.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, the act of regulating cryptocurrency can be misinterpreted.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The layman may perceive the Government endorsing cryptocurrency investments and giving it a stamp of approval.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many may also question whether regulating DPTs makes it legal tender.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Notwithstanding, some businesses in Singapore already accept cryptocurrency payments.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What if the cryptocurrency somehow loses its value and status and businesses decide that they no longer want to accept it as a payment form?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What if the issuing company for the DPT goes bust?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What happens to customers who stocked up on the cryptocurrency, believing that it could always come in handy for real-world transactions?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Would the Government monitor the situation and intervene to prevent such situations?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And since it is an individual decision, how can the Government moderate this area?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Imagine if one had signed a two-year lease in January 2019 for an apartment, agreeing to pay a quarter bitcoin per month.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The value of the bitcoin soared in the later part of that year.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This tenant would be paying more and more each month.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This will be more than a six-fold increase over the two years.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Government cannot regulate the value of cryptocurrency.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But what about businesses that accept cryptocurrency as a payment method, especially for long-term contracts for payment instalments?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And if a dispute arises, as in this example, what is the legal redress?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These scams are much like the online financial scams that we have seen a rise in Singapore in the past year, only that the funds involved are in cryptocurrency.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Unsuspecting victims have been tricked into becoming money mules by scammers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Such victims accept funds into their own bank accounts and deposit a portion into a crypto kiosk.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: An increased interest in cryptocurrency would also mean that more amateurs would dabble recklessly in cryptocurrency.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is particularly so in the current climate when people are grappling with job and income losses.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They may turn to cryptocurrencies as a get rich quick scheme.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is particularly so with recent news about the bitcoin hitting all-time high prices.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There are various irresponsible marketing content on the Internet promising consumers an "instant way to get rich".

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Fraudulent investments would have criminals pitching a new and developing cryptocurrency, such as an ICO, offering large monetary returns for a short-term, small investment.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In reality, the investment money is swallowed for personal gain.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Excuses about the complexities of cryptocurrency will be used to keep customers in the dark.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Earlier, Member Ms Ng Ling Ling raised a similar concern.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They are often the favourite targets of digital investment fraud.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Retirees are always interested in passive ways to grow their income.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I already have seniors asking me about investment in cryptocurrencies during my house visits.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They are getting familiar with digitalisation and online payment tools.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Credit to campaigns like the Seniors Go Digital movement.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, there are still areas where seniors are not particularly knowledgeable about, which renders them vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is especially so if scammers hook them with phrases like "Government-regulated".

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These scams usually start off focusing on the growth rates of various cryptocurrencies, while neglecting to highlight the high degree of volatility.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Once they have their interest, they may persuade victims to grant them access to remote-desktop tools or their personal information.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Thereafter, they steal their information to commit other cybercrimes, or have them transfer funds to cryptocurrency wallets that the victim does not have access to.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Our concern is not only about the law-abiding citizens, but those who are scammers looking to conceal their ill-gotten gains.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Bitcoin transactions are, in fact, transparent and logged into a public ledger which anyone can access.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These transactions can be traced right back to the day they are mined, which is helpful for law enforcers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, reconciling transactions across individual and private ledgers to individuals requires a lot of time and resources.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Would only crypto assets that are transparent be eligible for licensing?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Do Government agencies have the powers to confiscate ill-gotten gains in digital wallets?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can they freeze cryptocurrency accounts as they could with banks?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Its growing popularity will attract blockchain developer talents and those who want to do good with it.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Conversely, it can also attract scammers and crooks looking to make a quick buck.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Customers are also seeking payment solutions that will reduce their pain points, especially for cross-border transactions and one-stop solutions that are well-integrated throughout the entire payments value chain.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Banks have historically enjoyed a defensible moat of consumer trust.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: A US digital payments survey indicates that consumers are more comfortable entrusting their financial transactions to non-banking entities.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: And as this landscape continues to evolve and customer patterns shift, what can we do to ensure consumers continue to be protected?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We must have a keen understanding of how valuable customer data is to businesses.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: As important the customer is to the business, how we protect the consumer is also of paramount importance.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In the world of cloud computing, payments as a service, banking as a service and the rise of APIs, customer data is often traded and analysed to offer more curated services and products for value capture.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We need to ensure that deviations from the additional requirements can be audited, detected and enforced.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Trust is a key attribute for a successful financial eco-system and digital payment plays a significant role.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Every entity in the eco-system plays a role of shared responsibility.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Most if not all the additional requirements stated in section 21A are meant to build trust within the Singapore digital payment eco-system.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Today, many new digital companies have an outreach of millions of B2B and B2C customers.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: They are well positioned to provide financial services traditionally provided by incumbent banks.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: These digital companies either partner with banks to build their networks or directly compete with them.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Banks are also quickly evolving to build partnerships and develop their own customer-centric eco-systems.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We must be cognisant of the competitive and ever-evolving digital payment landscape.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: For our survival and relevance to the world, we must ensure that there is fairness, accountability and transparency and yet have the agility to safeguard the reputation and competitiveness of the Singapore financial eco-system – to be a home for future global fintech champions.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Many have called Bitcoin and cryptocurrencies a massive bubble, but fast forward to today, as alluded by other Members of this House, industry players see 2020 as a year where Bitcoin was perhaps being institutionalised.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is a further testimony to how banks and institutional investors, both local and abroad, are trying to keep up with the times to ensure that they remain relevant in the financial service offerings.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, the recent approval of the new digital banking licences in December is indicative that Singapore is taking a leap forward in attempting to become even more competitive as a global financial hub.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Against this backdrop, it is heartening to note that the MAS is also very quick to update the Payment Services Act 2019 so as to strengthen the regulatory frameworks, especially with regards to anti-money laundering and countering terrorism financing.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I understand that the MAS has a list of admission criteria but these are not meant to be exhaustive.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Will the Minister provide greater clarity as to the factors and their respective weightings in MAS' considerations in granting or rejecting PSA licensees?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: More importantly, what is the number of applicants at the various stages of approval and what is holding back MAS from approving or rejecting these applications?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Is the team overseeing the approvals adequately staffed to support the timely developments in this arena?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: On that note, I would also like to seek clarifications on some of the proposed amendments to the Payment Services Act.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The first is with regard to user protection measures.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Section 21 of the amendment gives MAS the power to impose user protection measures.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, there is no clarity for now as to what these measures might be at the moment, although MAS will consult the public and the industry on any implementation of such measures.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: MAS has also highlighted in an April 2020 FAQ paper that it does not intend to provide any regulatory safeguards for investments in digital payments, the safety and soundness of DPT service providers or the proper processing of DPT transactions.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In light of concerns surrounding business failures and cybersecurity, I believe a clear framework should be adopted and put in place as a pre-emptive measure, which aims to imbue users with greater confidence in the payment service infrastructure in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: A wider adoption of digitalisation can only be built up when consumers have adequate trust that the system works and that adequate circuit breakers or minimal fail safes are present to mitigate any damage.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: An example of which is the deposit insurance scheme in the case of monies in banks.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: A balance has to be struck, however, as mentioned by my colleague Leon Perera.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: There is the perception that increased regulatory powers by MAS may spark fears of over-regulation and excessively stifle innovation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In this regard, both end users and companies could benefit from greater regulatory and operational clarity sooner rather than later.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The second point I would like to highlight is with regards to the potential upward revision of the current limits on e-wallet users.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: According to MAS, these limits are in place to safeguard the risk of excess monetary outflows from bank deposits to non-bank e-money.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: With the signing of the new trade agreement with the UK, MAS has said that it would review these payment limits.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Because a higher limit would mean that firms can potentially offer more services to their customers, which in turn, encourages wider adoption and usage of digital payments in line with our hope for developing a Smart Nation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: With COVID-19, we have been forced to adopt digital contact tracing, which, much like digital payments, make use of the scanning of QR codes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I am sure Members would agree with me that the scanning of SafeEntry QR codes is now second nature to Singapore residents.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Yet the uptake for digital payment remains low as compared to a country like, say, China, where the authorities had to intervene to ensure that merchants still accept cash as a mode of payment – quite the opposite of Singapore's experience today, with "Cash Only" signs still quite commonplace at small businesses in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I note that the SG Digital Office was established in May 2020 under IMDA, but beyond Hawkers Go Digital or Seniors Go Digital, we could perhaps ask ourselves, why is it that the uptake of digital payment still remains low in Singapore and if more can be done to encourage the uptake of digital payment in the near future.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: At the same time, of course, let us not forget that the older generation might not be as proficient technologically and we should push for progress while also being cognisant of not leaving anyone behind.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I applaud the new amendments which will build consumer confidence in the use of digital payments while encouraging a robust e-payment eco-system.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Government's position on regulating digital tokens, specifically cryptocurrency, has garnered a significant amount of interest.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Cryptocurrencies are now required to be protected and each cryptocurrency transaction must be processed properly.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is also good news for technology start-ups which view cryptocurrencies, particularly Initial Coin Offerings or ICOs, as a quick way to fund their innovations.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Government's move to take an active stance to regulate and safeguard customers' virtual assets will encourage more to partake in new technology businesses.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I wish to raise my concerns on a few topics: first, cybersecurity issues about cryptocurrency; second, social engineering problems; third, manipulation of crypto exchanges and issuance of digital tokens.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Even with licensing and regulations, crypto exchanges are fraught with risks and liabilities.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Any financial activity that takes place through cyberspace would be a target for cybercriminals.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Crypto exchanges are hot targets for hackers and losses by the millions have captured headlines in the past five years.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Although the security systems designed to protect the exchanges and customers have been enhanced over the years, the plunder by hackers continued through the past year.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Half of crypto-related hacks are reportedly from DeFi protocols and exchanges.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These are financial services using smart contracts, which are automated enforceable agreements that do not need intermediaries like a bank or a lawyer.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The concept has grown in popularity in the past year but they are also controversial because they are attractive to criminal hackers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Cryptocurrencies, too, are subject to cyberattack methodologies like phishing and data breaches.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Hackers can exploit cross-site scripting issues to change a customer's withdrawal address and draw money from the customer's account into their own – according to a Forbes article about the risks of crypto exchanges.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As both accounts are legitimate, these activities would resemble normal transactions and it may take some time before the illegal activity is flagged.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: By then, it may be too late for any action.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Two-factor authentication, or 2FA, is widely considered the gold standard for protecting online accounts.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Yet, in the case of a server-side vulnerability in a crypto exchange, hackers can bypass 2FA checks entirely through remote code execution, or RCE.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A research revealed in December 2017 that nearly 90% of all RCE attacks are driven by crypto-mining.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Fortunately, there are ways to identify crypto exchanges which are relatively secure and safe to work with.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When cryptocurrency was largely unregulated, customers were required to do their own extensive research, which often requires deep reading and technical knowledge.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With enhanced regulations for the industry, I hope the Government is also taking into consideration security factors when granting or renewing the licenses.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, crypto exchanges must present adequate security measures before they are licensed.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These would include security audits of smart contracts and front-end application servers and regular bug bounty programmes to stay ahead of hackers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I hope this will open up more opportunities for local white hackers and cybersecurity talents to hone their skills and land good jobs and development opportunities in the industry.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Besides cyberattacks, frauds and social engineering are challenges to contend with, as with any online financial activities and transactions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The past year saw an uptick in victims being scammed or unwittingly involved in Ponzi schemes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Moreover, online criminals have devised all kinds of complex methodologies to attack crypto exchanges from multiple fronts, not only targeting the exchanges but also customers and third-party service providers associated with the exchanges.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A recent example was a cyberattack on several cryptocurrency websites after employees at a hosting company were targeted and socially engineered to give access to the targeted websites.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Although no funds were lost, the hacker was believed to have obtained personal information and documents from the user database.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These included sensitive information like government-issued IDs, addresses and passwords.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Unrelated to cybersecurity, but also having an insidious impact on the stability of crypto exchanges, is crypto market manipulation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Back in 2019, allegations on cryptocurrency exchanges manipulating data to attract traders to their platforms had rocked the industry.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A series of crackdowns alleviated this problem, but it is still present to a lesser degree.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is commonly cited as the equivalent as the "pump-and-dump" securities fraud in the stock market.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As all these variables continue to plague the crypto exchanges, I am particularly concerned about the inevitable surge in interest from newcomers once the new regulations come into effect.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They may be lulled into a false sense of security and invest recklessly.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We may also see a rise in cybercrimes if victims fail to adopt all the necessary precautions to protect their assets.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We can license and regulate, but the volatility of the industry means that reviewing the laws must be an on-going and frequent process.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Anyone who wants to participate must continuously educate themselves and stay abreast with news on the technology.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am pleased to note that there are several crypto and blockchain courses available in Singapore and some are under SkillsFuture.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Given the complexity of cryptocurrency investment, some may prefer to turn to corporate finance advisers, who have shown increasing interest in offering clients exposure to cryptocurrency.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To what extent are they allowed to facilitate crypto transactions for clients, and would they require a special licence for such activities?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It would be good to know if there is proper credentialing for financial advisers who want to market cryptocurrency to customers as an investment.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I now move to my last topic on token issuance.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Ultimately, we want to strike a fine balance between accessibility and security.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We want to encourage our tech entrepreneurs to leverage on a vibrant fintech economy, while maintaining stability and security through anti-money laundering and cybersecurity regulations.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Moreover, well-regulated developments in the industry will serve to stimulate other areas like technology advancements and cybersecurity, which in turn, creates employment.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There were quite a number of comments about protecting consumers, protecting seniors, educating the public on the risk of DPTs or digital payment tokens.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But there are also others who commented that we should not over-regulate and we have to encourage entrepreneurship.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is in essence what this Bill is about, to strike that balance, and in that process, take a risk-differentiated approach.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: First, let me deal with the risks that the Bill mainly seeks to address – money laundering, terrorism financing and other illegal activities.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Louis Ng suggested sharing more information and feedback with financial institutions to improve the efficacy of suspicious transaction reporting.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Louis Ng asked his question in the context of identifying illegal wildlife trade, but really, the broader purpose is to counter all illegal activities in general.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Financial institutions are required to report suspicious transactions to the Suspicious Transaction Reporting Office in the Singapore Police Force.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Relevant agencies have shared case studies and red flag indicators on risks with financial institutions to help them better detect and report these illicit activities.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Agencies also provide feedback to financial institutions to sharpen their efforts in reporting suspicious transactions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, the efforts as suggested by Mr Ng is on-going.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Don Wee also asked if there could be a centralised platform for DPT service providers to research on transaction details, share information and improve efficiency.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We agree with this suggestion, the principle of it.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MAS has been working with the industry and relevant associations, on the sharing of emerging risks and typologies, and best practices to collectively raise Anti-Money Laundering/Combating the Financing of Terrorism or AML/CFT standards, and improve their effectiveness and efficiency.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Louis Ng asked if there is a space for anonymised financial transactions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Usually, that is cash, that is the most anonymised.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But if it is digital, indeed, in this digitised world, everything we do, from buying something online to even surfing the net, we leave a digital trail that is in someone's possession.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And usually the data is used to push to you the next advertisement that you should take note of.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng also raised questions on whether these service providers would be required to identify and verify their customers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Payment service providers are also required to retain the necessary information on customers and transactions to maintain proper audit trails and facilitate investigations by law enforcement agencies.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Don Wee asked if MAS requires DPT service providers to use search engines, like in the maritime sector, to authenticate shipments.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MAS expects DPT service providers to apply a risk-based AML/CFT approach that is appropriate for the risks of their business and nature of transactions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Hence, MAS does not prescribe the use of specific systems.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: However, DPT service providers should take enhanced risk measures such as ascertaining the purpose of the transaction or source of funds using relevant sources of information when they encounter higher risk situations.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: He raised various instances where DPT service providers need not be subject to perhaps the full suite of regulatory measures.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These are valid concerns and indeed, we, as I explained earlier, that is why we take a risk-based, modular approach for the Payment Services Act.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And in fact, that defines the entire architecture of this Act.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For example, it is not the intent of the Payment Services Act to capture entities that conduct general marketing or advertising activities.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Whether an entity is caught by the Act, is dependent on the facts and circumstances of each case.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The exact rules will be spelled out in subsidiary legislation or guidelines on licensing for licensees; and we will consult the public and the industry as MAS do so.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I want to assure Mr Leon Perera that our rules are aligned to the FATF as well as international best practices.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This includes the regulation of cross-border remittance of monies.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: On monitoring cross-border flows that Mr Leon Perera asked, our rules require licensees to keep transaction records and we have supervisory oversight to review them.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, monitoring and enforcement is more ex post than ex ante.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And of course, we rely on active cooperation with foreign counterparts and sharing of intelligence.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Also, as mentioned by Mr Leon Perera, MAS has carved out from regulation, any payment service that is solely incidental to carrying on a business that is already regulated under the Securities and Futures Act.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: On the need to provide clearer definition of the word "incidental", it is already defined in the Payment Services Act, which is that a payment service is incidental if it is "to support the other business and provided by the person in connection with carrying on of the other business".

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If necessary, MAS can issue further guidance on this, as we receive more feedback from the industry.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Next, I will address crypto-related developments which were brought up by Mr Saktiandi and Mr Don Wee, specifically on stablecoins and decentralised finance or DeFi.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These services are still nascent in Singapore but it can change quickly.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: DeFi is currently the most common form of DPT services which will be captured with the expanded scope introduced today.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But if there is a need to evolve our regulatory regime further in future, we will be ready.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Next are questions on technology and cybersecurity risks, as well as data privacy standards.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Derrick Goh proposed differentiated technology and cybersecurity requirements for payment institutions, and in particular, for standard payment institutions to perform self-assessment of their technology and cyber risks.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The underlying principle behind Mr Goh's suggestion is that MAS should take a risk-based approach when applying technology and cyber security requirements on different types of financial institutions and we agree with this underlying principle.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Payment service providers must meet MAS' standards on technology risk management and cyber hygiene practices.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Examples of these regulatory requirements include establishing robust security controls to mitigate the risk of malware infection and data loss, and ensuring strong user authentication for systems that are used to access customer information.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: New entrants who are not able to meet these standards will not be allowed to commence business.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MAS imposes more stringent requirements on payment service providers as they become significant players in the payment industry.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Payment service providers are expected to independently perform risk assessment against these MAS requirements.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: However, as part of our on-going supervision, it is still necessary for MAS to periodically assess the cyber resilience of payment service providers by reviewing the effectiveness of their processes and controls.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
